html.title: HTML Tutorial
html.description: Learn HTML from basics to advanced.

lessons.title: HTML Introduction
lessons.content:
What is HTML?

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the standard markup language for creating web pages.

Example

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
<h1>Hello World</h1>
</body>
</html>
lessons.example: Hello World

lessons.title: HTML Elements
lessons.content:
HTML Elements

An HTML element is defined by a start tag, some content, and an end tag.

<tagname>Content goes here...</tagname>
lessons.example:
My First Heading

My first paragraph.

lessons.title: HTML Headings and Paragraphs
lessons.content:
Give your page a clear structure

Headings describe the sections of a page. Use <h1> for the main heading, then <h2> and <h3> for nested sections. Paragraphs use the <p> element.

Choose heading levels for meaning and structure, not just for their visual size.

Try changing the heading levels
lessons.example:
My garden journal

Notes from the backyard.

Things growing now

Tomatoes, basil, and snap peas.

lessons.title: HTML Links and Images
lessons.content:
Connect pages and add images

Links use the <a> element with an href destination. Images use <img>; provide useful alternative text with the alt attribute.

Make links descriptive

Link text such as “Read the field notes” tells people where the link goes, even when read out of context.
lessons.example:
Explore the coast

Read the field notes

lessons.title: HTML Lists
lessons.content:
Group related items

Use <ul> for an unordered list and <ol> when the order matters. Put each item inside an <li> element.

A checklist for a small project
lessons.example:
Weekend project

  1. Sketch an idea
  2. Build the first version
  3. Ask a friend to try it

Bring along

  • Notebook
  • Pencils

lessons.title: HTML Forms
lessons.content:
Collect information

Forms group controls for entering data. A <label> should describe each input. Matching the label’s for value to the input’s id makes the form easier to use.

This example is only the interface. Sending form data requires a server or another form handler.
lessons.example:
<form>
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com" required>
  <button type="submit">Join the list</button>
</form>

lessons.title: HTML Attributes
lessons.content:
Add information to elements

Attributes appear in an element's opening tag and provide extra information. They usually have a name and a value, such as href on a link or alt on an image.

Boolean attributes

Some attributes, such as required and disabled, work by being present on the element.
lessons.example: Open an example page

lessons.title: Semantic HTML
lessons.content:
Describe the purpose of your content

Semantic elements communicate what a region is for. Use <header> for introductory content, <nav> for navigation, <main> for the page's primary content, and <footer> for related closing information.

Semantic structure helps browsers, assistive technology, and other developers understand a page.
lessons.example:
Trail notes

Today's route

By the river

A quiet two-mile walk beneath the trees.

Written outdoors.

lessons.title: HTML Tables
lessons.content:
Present data in rows and columns

Tables are for data with meaningful row and column relationships, not for page layout. Use <th> for headings and <caption> to describe the table.
lessons.example:
Garden harvest
MonthTomatoes
July8
August14

lessons.title: HTML Audio and Video
lessons.content:
Add media with native controls

The <audio> and <video> elements let browsers play media. Add the controls attribute to give visitors playback controls and provide fallback text for unsupported formats.
lessons.example: Media on the web

lessons.title: Accessible HTML Basics
lessons.content:
Make pages work for more people

Start with native HTML: use buttons for actions, links for navigation, labels for inputs, and headings in a logical order. Give informative images useful alternative text and make sure controls can be reached with a keyboard.

Check your page

Try navigating with the Tab key and check that each control has a clear accessible name.
lessons.example: Choose a reminder

lessons.title: HTML Form Validation
lessons.content:
Guide the user before submission

HTML can validate common field requirements with attributes such as required, minlength, type, and pattern. This gives immediate feedback and reduces avoidable errors.
lessons.example:
<form>
  <label for="password">Password</label>
  <input id="password" type="password" minlength="8" required>
  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

lessons.title: Semantic HTML and SEO
lessons.content:
Structure content for humans and search engines

Semantic markup gives web pages meaning and clarity. Labels, headings, and descriptive link text help both users and search engines understand the purpose of each section.
lessons.example:
Spring planting guide

Learn which vegetables grow best in cool weather.

css.title: CSS Tutorial
css.description: Style your web pages with CSS.

lessons.title: CSS Introduction
lessons.content:
What is CSS?

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It describes how HTML elements are displayed.
lessons.example: Hello CSS

lessons.title: CSS Selectors
lessons.content:
Choose which elements to style

A type selector targets every element of a kind. A class selector starts with a dot and can be reused. An ID selector starts with a hash and should identify one unique element.

Try the class selector
lessons.example:
Field notes

The first seeds are in.

Next: water the seedlings.

lessons.title: CSS Colors and Text
lessons.content:
Set a visual tone

CSS can set text color, background color, font size, line height, and alignment. Hex values such as #087f5b give precise colors; named colors are handy for quick experiments.

Keep text comfortable to read

Pair a readable font size with enough line height and contrast against the background.
lessons.example:
A little color

Thoughtful type and contrast make a page easier to read.

lessons.title: The CSS Box Model
lessons.content:
Every element is a box

The box model is made of content, padding, border, and margin. Padding adds space inside the border; margin adds space outside it. box-sizing: border-box makes declared widths include padding and border.
lessons.example:
A tidy box

Padding is inside. Margin is outside.

lessons.title: CSS Flexbox
lessons.content:
Arrange items in a row or column

Set display: flex on a container to arrange its children. Use gap for consistent spacing, justify-content along the main axis, and align-items across it.
lessons.example: PlanBuildShare

lessons.title: CSS Grid
lessons.content:
Build two-dimensional layouts

CSS Grid arranges content in rows and columns. Define columns with grid-template-columns and use gap to space items consistently.

Flexible columns

The minmax() function sets a minimum and maximum track size; auto-fit lets columns wrap when space is limited.
lessons.example:
One
Two
Three

lessons.title: Responsive CSS
lessons.content:
Adapt layouts to available space

Responsive layouts use flexible widths and media queries to keep content usable on different screens. Start with a layout that works in a narrow column, then add a breakpoint when the content needs more room.

Resize the preview to see the card switch from one column to two.
lessons.example:
A smaller screen
A wider screen

lessons.title: CSS Pseudo-classes
lessons.content:
Style an element in a particular state

Pseudo-classes such as :hover, :focus-visible, and :first-child select elements based on how they are being used or where they appear.

Keep keyboard focus visible

A visible focus style helps people who navigate with a keyboard see where they are on the page.
lessons.example:
Read the details
  • First item
  • Second item

lessons.title: CSS Custom Properties
lessons.content:
Reuse values with CSS variables

Custom properties are declared with names that start with -- and read with var(). Declare shared values on :root so they are available throughout the document.
lessons.example: Update the variable once to change both elements.

lessons.title: CSS Positioning
lessons.content:
Control where elements sit

Static positioning follows normal document flow. Relative positioning adjusts an element from its normal spot. Absolute positioning uses a positioned ancestor as its reference, while fixed positioning stays attached to the viewport.
lessons.example:
NEW

Positioned in the frame

lessons.title: CSS Transitions
lessons.content:
Make state changes feel clear

A transition interpolates a CSS property when its value changes. Specify the property and duration, then define the changed value in a state such as :hover or :focus-visible.

Motion should support feedback. Keep an immediate focus indicator for keyboard users.
lessons.example:
<style>
button { padding: 12px 18px; border: 0; background: #087f5b; color: white; transition: background-color .2s ease, transform .2s ease; }
button:hover { background: #075d44; transform: translateY(-2px); }
button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #e77a63; outline-offset: 3px; }
</style>
<button type="button">Hover or focus me</button>

lessons.title: CSS Animations
lessons.content:
Add motion to a design

Animations use keyframes to control how styles change over time. They are useful for drawing attention to a state change, guiding a user, or creating a more polished interface.
lessons.example: New lesson

lessons.title: Designing for Dark Mode
lessons.content:
Support different visual preferences

Dark mode helps some users reduce eye strain and can feel more comfortable in low-light environments. You can create a theme by defining colors that work well together and contrast clearly.
lessons.example:
Evening view

Dark mode can improve comfort for long reading sessions.

javascript.title: JavaScript Tutorial
javascript.description: Make your pages interactive with JS.

lessons.title: JavaScript Introduction
lessons.content:
What is JavaScript?

JavaScript is the programming language of the web.
lessons.example: Hello

lessons.title: JavaScript Variables
lessons.content:
Store values with variables

Use const for a value that will not be reassigned and let when it needs to change. Strings hold text, numbers hold numeric values, and booleans are either true or false.

lessons.title: JavaScript Functions
lessons.content:
Reuse a set of instructions

A function groups work under a name. Parameters are inputs, and return sends a result back to the caller. Call the function whenever you need that result.

lessons.title: JavaScript Events
lessons.content:
Respond to a user's action

Events let a page respond to actions such as a click. Use addEventListener to connect an event to a function, keeping behavior separate from your HTML.
lessons.example: Click the button.

lessons.title: JavaScript Conditions
lessons.content:
Choose what your code does

An if statement runs a block when its condition is true. Add else for the alternative path. Comparison operators such as === check whether two values are equal.

lessons.title: JavaScript Arrays
lessons.content:
Keep a collection of values

An array stores an ordered list. Items use zero-based indexes, and the length property tells you how many items it contains. Methods such as push() add an item to the end.

lessons.title: JavaScript Loops
lessons.content:
Repeat work for each item

A for...of loop visits each value in an iterable such as an array. Use it when you want to perform the same task for every item.

lessons.title: JavaScript Objects
lessons.content:
Describe one thing with related values

Objects store named properties. Use dot notation when you know the property name, and bracket notation when the name is stored in a variable.

lessons.title: Working with the DOM
lessons.content:
Update a page with JavaScript

The Document Object Model (DOM) represents a page as objects that scripts can read and change. Select elements with methods such as querySelector(), then update text, attributes, or classes.

For text from users or other untrusted sources, prefer textContent over innerHTML.
lessons.example: Not started

lessons.title: JavaScript Form Events
lessons.content:
Handle form input

Listen for the form's submit event to respond when someone submits it. Call preventDefault() when you want to handle the action in the page instead of navigating away.

lessons.title: JavaScript Async Basics
lessons.content:
Handle time-based work

Some actions take time, such as fetching data or waiting for a timer. Promises and async/await help you write asynchronous code that is easier to follow.
lessons.example:
<script>
async function loadMessage() {
  return 'Data loaded';
}
loadMessage().then(message => console.log(message));
</script>

lessons.title: Handling Errors in JavaScript
lessons.content:
Expect the unexpected

Real code can fail. Use try and catch blocks to handle mistakes gracefully and keep the page usable even when something goes wrong.
lessons.example:
<script>
try {
  const result = JSON.parse('{bad json}');
  console.log(result);
} catch (error) {
  console.error('Could not parse the data.');
}
</script>

accessibility.title: Web Accessibility
accessibility.description: Build pages that are usable for everyone.

lessons.title: Why Accessibility Matters
lessons.content:
Design for more people

Accessible websites work better for everyone, not just people who use assistive technology. Clear structure, readable text, and sensible interactions make a page easier for all visitors to use.

Accessibility is a design quality, not a bonus feature.
lessons.example:
Community notice board

Friendly, clear information helps every visitor find what they need quickly.

lessons.title: Page Landmarks
lessons.content:
Use semantic regions

Landmarks help assistive technology understand where the header, navigation, main content, and footer live. Use <header>, <nav>, <main>, and <footer> to make the page structure clear.
lessons.example:
School garden

Plan

Planting schedule for the next week.

Updated each Monday.

lessons.title: Keyboard-Friendly Controls
lessons.content:
Support the keyboard users

People may navigate by pressing Tab, Enter, and Space instead of using a mouse. Ensure links, buttons, and form fields have clear focus states and can be reached in a logical order.

Quick check

Press Tab across the page and notice whether each interactive element is easy to identify.
lessons.example: View notes

lessons.title: Color and Contrast
lessons.content:
Make text easy to read

Strong contrast between text and background improves readability. Avoid low-contrast combinations such as pale gray text on a white background, and test your colors with accessibility tools or browser contrast checks.
lessons.example:
Clear contrast helps everyone read the content.

Join the event

lessons.title: Accessible Forms
lessons.content:
Label every form control

Every input should have a visible label and an associated for value. Use helpful placeholders only as extras, not as the only instruction. Error messages should clearly explain what to fix.
lessons.example:
<form>
  <label for="name">Full name</label>
  <input id="name" type="text" required>
  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

lessons.title: Focus States and Keyboard Navigation
lessons.content:
Make interactive elements obvious

Keyboard users rely on visible focus styles to understand where they are on the page. A clear focus indicator, sensible tab order, and focusable controls make navigation much smoother.
lessons.example: Read more

lessons.title: Screen Reader Basics
lessons.content:
Write content that is understandable when read aloud

Screen readers announce headings, buttons, form labels, and links in a predictable way. Use concise wording, descriptive labels, and meaningful structure to support people who rely on assistive technology.
lessons.example:
Project notes

Review the latest draft before publishing.

git.title: Git and GitHub
git.description: Track changes, collaborate, and manage projects with confidence.

lessons.title: Git Introduction
lessons.content:
What is Git?

Git helps you save snapshots of your project as it changes. It keeps a history of work, lets you compare versions, and makes team collaboration much easier.

A repository is a project folder with version history attached.
lessons.example:
git init
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"

lessons.title: Making a Commit
lessons.content:
Save a meaningful checkpoint

A commit records the current state of your files. Write a short message that explains what changed so future you and your teammates can understand the project history.
lessons.example:
git add index.html
git commit -m "Add homepage layout"

lessons.title: Branching Basics
lessons.content:
Work on ideas separately

Branches let you try new changes without disturbing the main project. This is useful for experiments, bug fixes, and feature work that need their own timeline.
lessons.example:
git checkout -b feature/contact-form
# make changes
git checkout main

lessons.title: Merging Changes
lessons.content:
Combine work together

When a feature is ready, you merge the branch back into the main branch. This brings the finished changes into the active project while keeping the update history visible.
lessons.example:
git checkout main
git merge feature/contact-form

lessons.title: Using GitHub
lessons.content:
Share and collaborate

GitHub hosts repositories online and makes it easier to review code, discuss changes, and contribute to projects with others. Pull requests are a common way to propose updates.
lessons.example:
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/project.git
git push -u origin main

lessons.title: Pull Requests
lessons.content:
Review work before merging

A pull request is a proposal to merge changes from one branch into another. It makes it easier to discuss updates, review code, and catch issues before the change is accepted.
lessons.example:
git checkout feature/contact-form
git push origin feature/contact-form
# open pull request on GitHub

lessons.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
lessons.content:
Fix overlapping changes carefully

Merge conflicts happen when two people edit the same part of a file. Read both versions, decide which content should remain, and then save a final version that combines the right changes.
lessons.example:
git checkout main
git merge feature/contact-form
# fix conflict markers in files
git add .
git commit

apis.title: APIs and JSON
apis.description: Learn how data moves between apps and websites.

lessons.title: What is an API?
lessons.content:
Connect programs together

An API is a way for one application to request information or actions from another. On the web, APIs often send data as JSON, which is a lightweight format for structured information.
lessons.example:
{
  "name": "Maya",
  "course": "Web Development"
}

lessons.title: Fetching Data
lessons.content:
Ask for data from a server

The fetch() function lets JavaScript request data from a URL. It returns a Promise, which you can use to handle success and error cases.
lessons.example:
<script>
fetch('https://api.example.com/users')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data));
</script>

lessons.title: Working with JSON
lessons.content:
Read structured data

JSON stores data as key-value pairs inside objects and arrays. It is easy to parse in JavaScript and perfect for sending information between a front-end app and a backend service.
lessons.example:
<script>
const student = { name: 'Ava', enrolled: true, lessons: ['HTML', 'CSS'] };
console.log(student.lessons[0]);
</script>

lessons.title: HTTP Status Codes
lessons.content:
Know if a request worked

Status codes tell you whether a server understood your request. A 200 means success, while 404 means the resource was not found and 500 means the server failed.
lessons.example:
200 OK
404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error

lessons.title: Handling API Errors
lessons.content:
Prepare for problems

Network errors, invalid responses, and server outages happen. Check the response status and show a safe fallback message so users still know what is happening.
lessons.example:
<script>
fetch('/api/profile')
  .then(response => {
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Profile unavailable');
    return response.json();
  })
  .catch(error => console.error(error.message));
</script>

lessons.title: CRUD Basics
lessons.content:
Manage create, read, update, and delete actions

Most APIs support CRUD operations. These are the basic actions used to create records, read them, update existing values, and delete them when they are no longer needed.
lessons.example:
GET /users
POST /users
PUT /users/1
DELETE /users/1

lessons.title: API Authentication
lessons.content:
Protect data and requests

Some APIs require authentication so only authorized users can read or change certain data. Common methods include API keys, tokens, and OAuth flows that verify identity before access is granted.
lessons.example: Authorization: Bearer your-token-here

projects.title: Beginner Project Track
projects.description: Build small web projects from idea to launch.

lessons.title: Start with a Simple Idea
lessons.content:
Choose a focused project

Small projects work best when they solve one clear problem. A simple task, such as a to-do list or a personal landing page, is easier to finish and learn from.
lessons.example:
Project goal

Create a page that lets a user add and remove tasks.

lessons.title: Plan the Layout
lessons.content:
Sketch before building

Outline the page structure first: header, main content, controls, and footer. A quick wireframe helps you decide what content needs to exist before writing code.
lessons.example:
Header

  • Task one

lessons.title: Build the First Version
lessons.content:
Turn the plan into code

Start with the basic HTML structure, add CSS for layout and color, then use JavaScript to make elements interactive. Aim for a working version before polishing details.
lessons.example:
<form>
  <input type="text" placeholder="New task">
  <button>Add</button>
</form>

lessons.title: Test and Improve
lessons.content:
Check the experience

Open the page in a browser and test each interaction. Try the happy path, then look for edge cases such as empty inputs, confusing labels, or missing feedback.
lessons.example: Click the button with an empty field and check whether the page shows a helpful message.

lessons.title: Share the Project
lessons.content:
Publish and learn

When the project works, share it with friends, family, or classmates. Each project teaches a new pattern and gives you something to talk about in your portfolio or resume.
lessons.example:
Live project

Published on GitHub Pages or another free hosting service.

roadmap.title: Beginner Frontend Roadmap
roadmap.description: A step-by-step path from HTML basics to building and publishing your first project.

lessons.title: 1. Learn HTML Foundations
lessons.content:
Structure the page

Start by learning how HTML gives meaning to each part of a webpage. Understand headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, and form controls before moving on to styling and interaction.
lessons.example:
Welcome

My first webpage is taking shape.

Learn more

lessons.title: 2. Build Layouts with CSS
lessons.content:
Shape the visual design

Use CSS to control color, spacing, layout, and typography. Once you understand selectors and the box model, you can create attractive and readable page layouts.
lessons.example:
My design

Clean layout makes content easier to read.

lessons.title: 3. Make It Responsive
lessons.content:
Adapt to different screen sizes

Responsive design ensures your pages look good on phones, tablets, and desktops. Use flexible layouts, media queries, and readable spacing to improve the user experience.

A page should feel comfortable whether someone opens it on a laptop or a small phone screen.
lessons.example:
Card one
Card two

lessons.title: 4. Add Interactivity with JavaScript
lessons.content:
Teach the page to react

JavaScript allows you to respond to clicks, gather input, and update the page dynamically. Learn variables, functions, conditions, arrays, and DOM changes to build interactive features.
lessons.example: Ready to begin.

lessons.title: 5. Learn Git and GitHub
lessons.content:
Track work and collaborate

Use Git to save versions of your code and GitHub to share projects online. Branches, commits, and pull requests help you manage work as your confidence grows.
lessons.example:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Create first version"
git push origin main

lessons.title: 6. Connect to APIs
lessons.content:
Bring in real data

APIs let your site request information from a server. Learn JSON, fetch requests, and error handling so your app can show live or dynamic content.
lessons.example:
<script>
fetch('/api/tutorials')
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data));
</script>

lessons.title: 7. Build Accessible Pages
lessons.content:
Design for everyone

Good frontend work includes accessibility. Make forms clear, use semantic HTML, support keyboard controls, and check color contrast so more people can use your site.
lessons.example:
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">

lessons.title: 8. Ship Your First Project
lessons.content:
Apply everything in context

Combine your HTML, CSS, JavaScript, design, and accessibility skills in a small project. Then publish it and reflect on what you learned so the next project is even stronger.
lessons.example:
Portfolio project

Home page, about section, contact form, and a polished landing screen.

project-challenges.title: Project Challenges
project-challenges.description: Practice by building small front-end projects with real constraints.

lessons.title: Challenge 1: Build a Landing Page
lessons.content:
Create a strong first impression

Design a simple landing page for a product, club, or personal brand. Include a headline, supporting text, call-to-action button, a feature list, and at least one image or graphic.

Checklist

  • Clear section headings
  • Readable spacing
  • Responsive layout
  • Consistent color palette
lessons.example:
Start your next project

Build, learn, and share your ideas.

lessons.title: Challenge 2: Build a To-Do App
lessons.content:
Practice interactivity

Create a page where a user can add a task, mark it complete, and delete it. Use JavaScript to update the list whenever the user interacts with the page.

Bonus

Add local storage so the tasks stay after a refresh.
lessons.example:
• Review notes
  • Finish project

lessons.title: Challenge 3: Build a Dashboard
lessons.content:
Organize information clearly

Design a dashboard with a header, summary cards, and a content area that displays activity or metrics. Focus on layout, hierarchy, and visual balance.

Constraints

Use a grid-based layout and keep all content easy to scan.
lessons.example:
Navigation
Visits: 520Sales: $2k

lessons.title: Challenge 4: Build a Quiz App
lessons.content:
Test your JavaScript logic

Make a small quiz with multiple-choice questions, a score counter, and a restart button. This helps practice conditions, arrays, loops, and user feedback.
lessons.example: Question 1

lessons.title: Challenge 5: Create a Portfolio
lessons.content:
Show your best work

Build a small portfolio page with sections for your projects, skills, and contact details. It should feel polished, readable, and professional without being overly complicated.
lessons.example:
Alex Carter

Front-end developer

Projects

quiz.title: Frontend Quick Quiz
quiz.description: Short recap questions to test the basics of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

lessons.title: HTML Quick Quiz
lessons.content:
Which tag creates a main heading?

Pick the best answer.

  • A. <header>
  • B. <h1>
  • C. <div>
  • D. <strong>
lessons.example: Main heading

lessons.title: CSS Quick Quiz
lessons.content:
What CSS property changes the space between elements?

Think about spacing and layout.

  • A. color
  • B. margin
  • C. border-radius
  • D. font-size
lessons.example:
<style>
.card { margin: 16px; }
</style>

lessons.title: JavaScript Quick Quiz
lessons.content:
Which keyword should you use for a value that should not be reassigned?

Choose the correct one.

  • A. var
  • B. let
  • C. const
  • D. static
lessons.example:
<script>
const name = 'Ava';
</script>

sql.title: SQL Tutorial
sql.description: Learn to query, organize, and safely update relational data with SQL.

lessons.title: 1. What Is SQL?
lessons.content:
Talk to relational databases

SQL is a language for defining, reading, and changing data stored in tables. A table has named columns and rows of related values.
lessons.example: CREATE TABLE books (id INTEGER, title TEXT);

lessons.title: 2. Read Data with SELECT
lessons.content:
Choose the columns you need

SELECT returns columns from a table. Use * for every column while exploring, then name columns explicitly in application queries.
lessons.example: SELECT title, author FROM books;

lessons.title: 3. Filter Rows with WHERE
lessons.content:
Find matching records

WHERE filters rows using comparisons and logical operators. Text values are written in single quotes.
lessons.example: SELECT title FROM books WHERE year >= 2020 AND genre = 'science';

lessons.title: 4. Sort and Limit Results
lessons.content:
Control result order

ORDER BY sorts results; DESC reverses the default ascending order. LIMIT caps the number of returned rows.
lessons.example: SELECT title, year FROM books ORDER BY year DESC LIMIT 10;

lessons.title: 5. Count and Summarize
lessons.content:
Calculate across rows

Aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, and AVG summarize many rows into a result.
lessons.example: SELECT COUNT(*) AS book_count, AVG(year) AS average_year FROM books;

lessons.title: 6. Group Results
lessons.content:
Summarize each category

GROUP BY creates groups for aggregate calculations. Use HAVING to filter groups after aggregation.
lessons.example: SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS total FROM books GROUP BY genre HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

lessons.title: 7. Combine Tables with JOIN
lessons.content:
Connect related records

A join matches rows across tables using related columns, commonly a primary key and a foreign key. An inner join returns only matching rows.
lessons.example: SELECT books.title, authors.name FROM books JOIN authors ON books.author_id = authors.id;

lessons.title: 8. Use a Subquery
lessons.content:
Use one query inside another

A subquery can provide values to an outer query. Keep queries readable by giving calculated columns and tables clear names.
lessons.example: SELECT title FROM books WHERE author_id IN (SELECT id FROM authors WHERE country = 'Canada');

lessons.title: 9. Add Rows with INSERT
lessons.content:
Create new records

INSERT INTO names the destination columns and the values for one or more new rows. Explicit column lists help prevent mistakes.
lessons.example: INSERT INTO books (title, author_id, year) VALUES ('River Stories', 3, 2024);

lessons.title: 10. Change Rows with UPDATE
lessons.content:
Update only intended records

UPDATE changes values in existing rows. Always check the WHERE condition first; without it, every row may be changed.
lessons.example: UPDATE books SET year = 2025 WHERE id = 12;

lessons.title: 11. Remove Rows with DELETE
lessons.content:
Delete carefully

DELETE removes matching rows. Preview the same condition with SELECT before deleting important data.
lessons.example: DELETE FROM books WHERE id = 12;

lessons.title: 12. Add Data Constraints
lessons.content:
Protect data consistency

Constraints enforce rules such as unique identifiers, required values, and valid relationships between tables.
lessons.example: CREATE TABLE authors (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE);

lessons.title: 13. Design Tables and Indexes
lessons.content:
Structure data for reliable queries

Choose columns that represent one fact each and use keys to identify records. Index columns used frequently for lookup, while remembering that indexes add storage and slow some writes.
lessons.example: CREATE INDEX books_author_id_idx ON books (author_id);

lessons.title: 14. Use Transactions
lessons.content:
Keep related changes together

A transaction groups multiple statements so they can succeed together or be rolled back. This is useful when one operation updates several related records.
lessons.example: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 25 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 25 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT;

lessons.title: 15. Write Safe Queries
lessons.content:
Keep user input separate from SQL

Build application queries with parameterized statements instead of joining user input into SQL text. Parameters help prevent injection and handle values correctly.
lessons.example: SELECT id, title FROM books WHERE author_id = ?;

express.title: Express.js Tutorial
express.description: Build Node.js web servers and APIs with Express.

lessons.title: 1. What Is Express?
lessons.content:
A web framework for Node.js

Express provides routing and middleware for HTTP servers. Start with a small application, then add features as your routes need them.

lessons.title: 2. Start a Server
lessons.content:
Listen for requests

An Express app listens on a port and can send a response for each incoming request. Use an environment-provided port when deploying.
lessons.example:
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
app.listen(port, () => console.log('Server ready'));

lessons.title: 3. Define Routes
lessons.content:
Match HTTP methods and paths

Routes connect a method and URL path to a handler. Use GET for reading and choose other methods according to the change being made.

lessons.title: 4. Read Route Parameters
lessons.content:
Capture values from a path

Named route segments are available in req.params. Validate identifiers before using them to look up data.

lessons.title: 5. Read Query Strings
lessons.content:
Handle optional URL filters

Query string values are available in req.query, such as search terms and pagination options. Treat them as untrusted input and validate their types and ranges.

lessons.title: 6. Parse JSON Requests
lessons.content:
Accept JSON bodies

Register express.json() before routes that read request bodies. Set sensible request-size limits for public APIs.

lessons.title: 7. Understand Middleware
lessons.content:
Process requests in order

Middleware can inspect or change a request, send a response, or call next() to continue. Register middleware before the routes that depend on it.

lessons.title: 8. Serve Static Files
lessons.content:
Make browser assets available

express.static serves files such as HTML, CSS, and images from a directory. Keep private files outside the public directory.
lessons.example:
const path = require('path');
app.use(express.static(path.join(__dirname, 'public')));

lessons.title: 9. Organize Routes with Router
lessons.content:
Keep route modules manageable

An Express router groups related endpoints and can be mounted under a shared URL prefix. This keeps the main server file focused.

lessons.title: 10. Validate Request Data
lessons.content:
Check data at the boundary

Validate required fields, formats, and allowed values before using request data. Return a clear client error for invalid input instead of trusting the browser.

lessons.title: 11. Handle Errors
lessons.content:
Return consistent failures

Pass asynchronous failures to error-handling middleware and keep error responses separate from internal stack traces. Register the error handler after routes.

lessons.title: 12. Work with Async Handlers
lessons.content:
Handle asynchronous work reliably

Database and network operations are asynchronous. Make sure rejected promises reach your error handler rather than becoming unhandled errors.

lessons.title: 13. Configure an App
lessons.content:
Keep environment-specific values outside code

Read ports and secrets from environment variables. Do not commit credentials, and provide safe configuration for local development and deployment.
lessons.example:
const port = Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000;
const mode = process.env.NODE_ENV || 'development';

lessons.title: 14. Secure an Express App
lessons.content:
Reduce common risks

Use HTTPS in production, validate input, limit request sizes, and apply appropriate security headers and rate limits. Never expose private data in error messages.
lessons.example:
app.use(express.json({ limit: '100kb' }));
// Add a maintained security-header middleware in production.

lessons.title: 15. Test and Deploy
lessons.content:
Prepare a dependable service

Test routes for success and failure cases, log useful operational details, and make the server use the host-provided port. Confirm the start command works before deploying.

react.title: React.js Tutorial
react.description: Build interactive user interfaces with React components and state.

lessons.title: 1. What Is React?
lessons.content:
Build interfaces from components

React lets you describe a user interface as reusable components. The UI updates when component data changes.

lessons.title: 2. Create Components
lessons.content:
Start with small pieces

A component is a JavaScript function that returns UI. Component names begin with a capital letter and can be composed together.

lessons.title: 3. Write JSX
lessons.content:
Describe markup in JavaScript

JSX looks like HTML but is transformed by the build tool. Use braces to include JavaScript expressions and close every element.
lessons.example:
const name = 'Mina'; const heading =

Hello, {name}

;

lessons.title: 4. Pass Data with Props
lessons.content:
Customize reusable components

Props are inputs supplied by a parent component. Treat props as read-only and give components clear, descriptive prop names.

lessons.title: 5. Store Changing Values with State
lessons.content:
Let interactions update the UI

The useState hook stores a value that can change over time. Call its setter to request a re-render instead of changing the value directly.

lessons.title: 6. Respond to Events
lessons.content:
Connect user actions to behavior

Pass event handlers such as onClick as functions. Do not call the handler while rendering unless that is intentional.

lessons.title: 7. Render Lists with Keys
lessons.content:
Turn arrays into UI

Use map to render a collection. Give each item a stable key so React can track additions, removals, and reordering.
lessons.example:
const fruits = ['Apple', 'Pear', 'Plum'];
    {fruits.map(fruit =>
  • {fruit}
    • )}

lessons.title: 8. Show UI Conditionally
lessons.content:
Render the state that applies

Use conditional expressions or early returns to show different content. Keep conditions readable, especially when the UI has multiple states.

lessons.title: 9. Build Forms
lessons.content:
Keep form values in sync

A controlled input gets its value from state and updates it with an event handler. Associate labels with inputs for accessible forms.
lessons.example:
const [email, setEmail] = useState('');

<label>Email <input value={email} onChange={event => setEmail(event.target.value)} /></label>

lessons.title: 10. Synchronize with Effects
lessons.content:
Use effects for external synchronization

useEffect is for synchronizing with systems outside rendering, such as browser APIs. Specify dependencies and clean up subscriptions or timers when needed.

lessons.title: 11. Load Data
lessons.content:
Represent loading, success, and error

When fetching data, show clear loading and error states as well as the completed result. Avoid updating a component after the request is no longer relevant.

lessons.title: 12. Share State Between Components
lessons.content:
Lift state to a common parent

If sibling components need the same changing value, keep that state in their closest shared parent and pass values and callbacks down as props.

lessons.title: 13. Use Context for Shared Values
lessons.content:
Avoid passing the same prop through many layers

Context can provide values such as a theme to distant descendants. Use it for genuinely shared data, not as a replacement for every prop.
lessons.example:
const ThemeContext = createContext('light');

<ThemeContext.Provider value='dark'>
  <App />
</ThemeContext.Provider>

lessons.title: 14. Make Components Accessible
lessons.content:
Use semantic browser controls

Prefer native buttons, links, labels, and headings. Ensure keyboard users can operate interactive elements and that controls have understandable names.
lessons.example:
<label htmlFor='name'>Name</label>
<input id='name' name='name' />
<button type='button'>Save</button>

lessons.title: 15. Build and Review a React App
lessons.content:
Combine components into a complete experience

Break a page into focused components, handle empty and error states, and test important interactions. Use the project build command to catch issues before publishing.

dart.title: Dart Tutorial
dart.description: Learn Dart syntax, types, collections, classes, and asynchronous programming.

lessons.title: 1. Meet Dart
lessons.content:
A language for apps and more

Dart is a typed programming language commonly used with Flutter. Dart programs start in a main function.

lessons.title: 2. Variables and Types
lessons.content:
Name and store values

Use var when the type can be inferred, final for a value assigned once, and const for a compile-time constant.

lessons.title: 3. Common Data Types
lessons.content:
Work with typed values

Dart includes types such as int, double, String, and bool. Types help tools catch mistakes before a program runs.

lessons.title: 4. Operators and Expressions
lessons.content:
Calculate and compare

Arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators combine values into expressions. Use parentheses to make complex calculations clear.
lessons.example:
final subtotal = 12.50 + 7.50;
final hasDiscount = subtotal >= 20 && true;

lessons.title: 5. Make Decisions and Repeat Work
lessons.content:
Control the order of execution

Use if and switch for decisions and loops to repeat work. Choose the loop that makes the stopping condition easy to understand.

lessons.title: 6. Write Functions
lessons.content:
Give reusable work a name

Functions can accept typed parameters and return a value. Use named parameters when they make a call easier to understand.

lessons.title: 7. Lists, Sets, and Maps
lessons.content:
Store groups of values

A list is ordered, a set stores unique values, and a map associates keys with values. Use collection methods to transform and inspect data.

lessons.title: 8. Understand Null Safety
lessons.content:
Handle values that may be absent

Dart types are non-nullable by default. Add ? when a value may be null, and check or provide a fallback before using it.

lessons.title: 9. Create Classes and Objects
lessons.content:
Model related data and behavior

Classes define fields and methods; objects are instances of those classes. Keep each class focused on one clear responsibility.

lessons.title: 10. Constructors and Initializers
lessons.content:
Initialize objects consistently

Constructors set up instances when they are created. Named constructors can describe different ways to create an object.

lessons.title: 11. Inheritance and Mixins
lessons.content:
Reuse behavior thoughtfully

Use inheritance when one type truly specializes another. Mixins can share behavior across classes without establishing a parent-child relationship.

lessons.title: 12. Enums and Generics
lessons.content:
Represent fixed choices and reusable types

Enums define a known set of options. Generics let classes and functions work with different types while preserving type checks.
lessons.example:
enum OrderStatus { pending, shipped, delivered }

T first<T>(List<T> items) => items.first;

lessons.title: 13. Handle Exceptions
lessons.content:
Respond to operations that fail

Use exceptions for exceptional failures, and catch only where your program can recover or add useful context. Avoid hiding failures with empty fallback values.

lessons.title: 14. Work Asynchronously with Futures
lessons.content:
Wait for a result without blocking

A Future represents a result that will be available later. Use async and await to write asynchronous code clearly.

lessons.title: 15. Packages and Tests
lessons.content:
Use the Dart ecosystem

Packages add reusable functionality through a project manifest. Write small tests for expected behavior and run the analyzer to catch issues early.

flutter.title: Flutter Tutorial
flutter.description: Build cross-platform apps with Flutter widgets and Dart.

lessons.title: 1. What Is Flutter?
lessons.content:
Create apps from a widget tree

Flutter is a UI toolkit for building applications across multiple platforms. You compose screens from widgets written in Dart.

lessons.title: 2. Create a Flutter Project
lessons.content:
Start with the Flutter tools

Create a project with the Flutter SDK, then run it on a selected device or emulator. The generated starter app is a useful place to explore the project structure.
lessons.example:
flutter create hello_app
cd hello_app
flutter run

lessons.title: 3. Understand the Widget Tree
lessons.content:
Compose the interface

Widgets describe configuration for parts of the UI. Build a tree of small widgets so each part has a clear purpose.
lessons.example: const Text('Hello, Flutter!');

lessons.title: 4. Build a Stateless Widget
lessons.content:
Use immutable screen configuration

A stateless widget is appropriate when its appearance depends only on its inputs. Override build to return its widget tree.

lessons.title: 5. Arrange Content with Layout Widgets
lessons.content:
Control space and alignment

Use widgets such as Row, Column, Padding, and Expanded to arrange children. Flutter layout is driven by constraints from parent to child.

lessons.title: 6. Build a Material App
lessons.content:
Set up app-level structure

MaterialApp provides common Material Design features, while Scaffold supplies a standard page structure such as an app bar and body.

lessons.title: 7. Manage Local State
lessons.content:
Update a screen after interaction

A stateful widget owns data that changes during its lifetime. Call setState when a change should rebuild that widget's UI.

lessons.title: 8. Handle User Input
lessons.content:
Respond to taps and text

Buttons expose callbacks for user actions, and text fields can use controllers or callbacks to read input. Dispose of controllers when their owning state is removed.

lessons.title: 9. Display Scrollable Lists
lessons.content:
Build lists efficiently

Use ListView.builder for longer or dynamic lists so items are created as they are needed. Provide stable keys when list items can change order.

lessons.title: 10. Navigate Between Screens
lessons.content:
Move through an app

Navigation pushes a new route onto a stack and can return a result when that route is popped. Choose a navigation structure that fits the number of app sections.

lessons.title: 11. Validate Forms
lessons.content:
Collect and validate user input

A Form groups fields and can validate them before submission. Give fields clear labels and explain validation errors in a helpful way.

lessons.title: 12. Load Asynchronous Data
lessons.content:
Show progress while waiting

Use a Future for one-time asynchronous work and represent loading, success, and error states in the UI.

lessons.title: 13. Themes and Assets
lessons.content:
Keep visuals consistent

Define shared colors and component styles in the app theme. Declare image and font assets in the project configuration before loading them.

lessons.title: 14. Responsive and Accessible UI
lessons.content:
Adapt to different people and screens

Use flexible layouts that respond to available space, provide meaningful labels for controls, and ensure text remains readable at larger sizes.

lessons.title: 15. Test and Release an App
lessons.content:
Check behavior before shipping

Test important widget interactions, run static analysis, and verify the app on target devices. Create a release build using the instructions for each platform.
lessons.example:
flutter analyze
flutter test
flutter build

php.title: PHP Tutorial
php.description: Learn PHP fundamentals, forms, databases, and safe server-side development.

lessons.title: 1. What Is PHP?
lessons.content:
Run code on the server

PHP is a server-side language often used to build dynamic websites. A PHP server processes a .php file and sends its response to the browser. MySchool's playground runs HTML, CSS, and JavaScript only, so these PHP examples are for learning and need a PHP server to execute.
lessons.example:
<?php
echo 'Hello, PHP!';
?>

lessons.title: 2. PHP Syntax and Output
lessons.content:
Write your first PHP statements

PHP code is placed between <?php and ?> tags. A semicolon ends most statements, and echo sends text into the response.
lessons.example:
<?php
echo 'Welcome to my site';
?>

lessons.title: 3. Variables and Data Types
lessons.content:
Store values for later use

PHP variables begin with $. PHP supports values including strings, integers, floats, booleans, arrays, and objects.
lessons.example:
<?php
$name = 'Amina';
$visits = 3;
$isMember = true;
echo $name;
?>

lessons.title: 4. Strings and Output
lessons.content:
Work with text

Use single or double quotes for strings. The dot operator joins strings; double-quoted strings can also interpolate variables. Escape untrusted text before displaying it in HTML.
lessons.example:
<?php
$name = 'Amina';
echo 'Hello, ' . htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');
?>

lessons.title: 5. Operators and Expressions
lessons.content:
Calculate and compare values

PHP includes arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators. Use strict comparisons such as === when you want both value and type to match.
lessons.example:
<?php
$price = 12.50;
$quantity = 2;
$total = $price * $quantity;
$isFree = $total === 0;
?>

lessons.title: 6. Make Decisions
lessons.content:
Choose what code should run

Use if, elseif, and else to branch based on a condition. A switch can make several discrete choices easier to read.
lessons.example:
<?php
$score = 82;
if ($score >= 80) {
    echo 'Great work';
} else {
    echo 'Keep practicing';
}
?>

lessons.title: 7. Repeat Work with Loops
lessons.content:
Run statements more than once

foreach is a convenient way to process each value in an array. Use a clear stopping condition with for and while loops.
lessons.example:
<?php
$topics = ['HTML', 'CSS', 'PHP'];
foreach ($topics as $topic) {
    echo htmlspecialchars($topic, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') . '<br>';
}
?>

lessons.title: 8. Work with Arrays
lessons.content:
Keep related values together

Indexed arrays store ordered values, while associative arrays use named keys. Arrays can be iterated, searched, and transformed with built-in functions.
lessons.example:
<?php
$student = [
    'name' => 'Amina',
    'course' => 'PHP',
];
echo $student['course'];
?>

lessons.title: 9. Write Functions
lessons.content:
Reuse named blocks of logic

Functions can accept typed parameters and return a value. Keep each function focused and give parameters and return values meaningful types.
lessons.example:
<?php
function greet(string $name): string
{
    return 'Hello, ' . $name;
}
echo greet('Amina');
?>

lessons.title: 10. Receive Form Data
lessons.content:
Handle browser form submissions

HTML forms send data using a method such as GET or POST. Read submitted values from the matching PHP superglobal, then validate them on the server; browser validation alone is not enough.
lessons.example:
<form method="post">
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" required>
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
<?php
if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] === 'POST') {
    $name = trim($_POST['name'] ?? '');
    echo htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');
}
?>

lessons.title: 11. Validate and Sanitize Input
lessons.content:
Do not trust submitted data

Validate that values have the expected format and range before using them. Escape output for its destination context; for HTML text, use htmlspecialchars.
lessons.example:
<?php
$email = filter_input(INPUT_POST, 'email', FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL);
if ($email === false || $email === null) {
    http_response_code(400);
    echo 'Enter a valid email address.';
}
?>

lessons.title: 12. Reuse Code with Includes
lessons.content:
Share common page parts

require and include load another PHP file. Use require when the application cannot continue without the file, and use explicit project-relative paths.
lessons.example:
<?php
require __DIR__ . '/includes/header.php';
?>
<main><h1>Course list</h1></main>
<?php
require __DIR__ . '/includes/footer.php';
?>

lessons.title: 13. Connect to a Database with PDO
lessons.content:
Use parameterized database queries

PDO provides a consistent interface to databases. Use prepared statements and bound parameters for values from users instead of concatenating input into SQL.
lessons.example:
<?php
$statement = $pdo->prepare(
    'SELECT id, title FROM posts WHERE author_id = :author_id'
);
$statement->execute(['author_id' => $authorId]);
$posts = $statement->fetchAll();
?>

lessons.title: 14. Use Sessions
lessons.content:
Keep small pieces of state between requests

Sessions can store information associated with a visitor across requests. Start the session before sending output, use secure cookie settings over HTTPS, and never store plain-text passwords in a session.
lessons.example:
<?php
session_start();
$_SESSION['display_name'] = 'Amina';
echo htmlspecialchars(
    $_SESSION['display_name'],
    ENT_QUOTES,
    'UTF-8'
);
?>

lessons.title: 15. Handle Errors and Build a Project
lessons.content:
Develop safely and verify your work

During development, enable useful error reporting; in production, log details privately and show users a safe message. Combine validation, templates, and database access into a small project, then test success and failure cases.
lessons.example:
<?php
try {
    $statement = $pdo->query('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM posts');
    $postCount = $statement->fetchColumn();
    echo 'Posts: ' . (int) $postCount;
} catch (PDOException $error) {
    error_log($error->getMessage());
    http_response_code(500);
    echo 'Unable to load posts right now.';
}
?>
